items.stem: Which is an assumption of the kinetic theory for an ideal gas?
options: the molecules have a large volume
there are no intermolecular forces between the molecules
items.answer: there are no intermolecular forces between the molecules
items.markingKey: Ideal gas: negligible molecular volume, no intermolecular forces, elastic collisions, random motion.

items.stem: Explain why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure.
items.answer: Molecules are close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the container volume, and intermolecular forces become significant.
items.markingKey: molecular volume significant [1]; intermolecular forces significant [1]

items.stem: Explain why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at low temperature.
items.answer: Molecules move more slowly, so intermolecular attractions have a greater effect and reduce the pressure exerted on the walls.
items.markingKey: slower molecules [1]; attractions significant [1]

items.stem: Under which conditions would a sample of methane behave most like an ideal gas?
items.answer: 500 kPa and 300 K
items.markingKey: Lowest pressure and highest temperature: molecules far apart and fast moving.

items.stem: Under which conditions would a sample of methane behave most like an ideal gas?
items.answer: 50 kPa and 300 K
items.markingKey: Lowest pressure and highest temperature: molecules far apart and fast moving.

items.stem: Diego compares the behaviour of helium and ammonia stored in cylinders in an AS practical class. (a) Explain why gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure. (b) Explain why ammonia deviates more from ideal behaviour than helium.
items.answer: (a) Molecules close together; molecular volume and intermolecular forces significant. (b) Ammonia has hydrogen bonding/polar; He atoms have very weak London forces.
items.markingKey: (a) Molecules close together; molecular volume and intermolecular forces significant. [2] (b) Ammonia has hydrogen bonding/polar; He atoms have very weak London forces. [2]

items.stem: Under which conditions does a real gas behave most like an ideal gas?
items.answer: high temperature and low pressure
items.markingKey: Molecules far apart (low p) and fast moving (high T): forces and molecular volume negligible.

items.stem: Which gas behaves least like an ideal gas at room temperature?
items.answer: ammonia
items.markingKey: NH₃ has hydrogen bonding (strong intermolecular forces).

items.stem: Explain why helium behaves more like an ideal gas than hydrogen chloride.
items.answer: He atoms are small with only 2 electrons, so very weak London forces; HCl is polar with permanent dipole forces.
items.markingKey: He weak forces/small [1]; HCl polar, stronger forces [1]

items.stem: Explain, in terms of molecules, why the pressure of a gas in a sealed container increases when it is heated.
items.answer: Molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide with the walls more often and with more force.
items.markingKey: faster molecules [1]; more frequent/forceful collisions [1]

items.stem: A student in Colombo claims that an ideal gas is one whose molecules attract each other strongly. Is the student correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. An ideal gas is assumed to have no intermolecular forces.
items.markingKey: identifies the error [1]; correct chemistry stated with reason [1]

items.stem: "Ammonia behaves more ideally than nitrogen because it has fewer electrons." Comment on this statement made by a student, correcting any error.
items.answer: The statement is incorrect. Ammonia has hydrogen bonding (strong forces), so it deviates more than nitrogen.

items.answer: m³

items.stem: Explain why the volatile-liquid (gas syringe) method gives a value of Mr that may be inaccurate for a liquid like ethanol near its boiling point.
items.answer: Near its boiling point the vapour does not behave ideally (strong intermolecular forces/hydrogen bonding), so pV = nRT does not apply exactly.
items.markingKey: non-ideal near boiling point [1]; intermolecular forces significant [1]

items.stem: Explain why temperatures must be in kelvin in pV = nRT.
items.answer: Volume and pressure are proportional to absolute temperature; the kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, so using °C gives wrong (even negative) values.
items.markingKey: proportional to absolute T [1]; °C gives wrong values [1]

items.stem: Which substance has a giant covalent structure?
items.answer: silicon(IV) oxide

items.stem: Explain why diamond is very hard but graphite is soft and slippery.
items.answer: In diamond each C is covalently bonded to four others in a rigid 3D network; in graphite layers are held by weak intermolecular forces and can slide.
items.markingKey: diamond 3D network of strong bonds [1]; graphite layers with weak forces between [1]

items.stem: Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.
items.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have higher charges (and are smaller) than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the electrostatic attraction between ions is stronger.
items.markingKey: higher charges/smaller ions [1]; stronger electrostatic attraction [1]

items.stem: Solid S has a melting point that is high. It does not conduct electricity when solid and conducts when molten or dissolved. It is soluble in water. Deduce the type of structure in S and explain each property.
items.answer: giant ionic (e.g. potassium bromide): strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice; ions are fixed in the solid but mobile when molten or dissolved.

items.stem: Explain why ice has a lower density than water.

items.stem: Explain why metals are malleable.

items.markingKey: (a) No: many strong covalent bonds throughout the structure must be broken to melt it. [2] (b) Open hydrogen-bonded lattice in ice; collapses on melting. [2]

items.stem: Why does a gas exert a pressure on its container?
options: molecules collide with the walls of the container
molecules are attracted to the walls
items.answer: molecules collide with the walls of the container
items.markingKey: Pressure = force per unit area from molecular collisions.

items.stem: Ana investigates how closely gases follow the ideal gas equation. Explain, in terms of molecules, why the pressure of a gas in a sealed container increases when it is heated.
items.answer: Molecules gain kinetic energy and move faster, so they collide with the walls more often and with more force.
items.markingKey: faster molecules; more frequent/forceful collisions [2]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at low temperature. (b) Explain why real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure.
items.answer: (a) Molecules move more slowly, so intermolecular attractions have a greater effect and reduce the pressure exerted on the walls. (b) Molecules are close together, so their own volume is no longer negligible compared with the container volume, and intermolecular forces become significant.
items.markingKey: (a) slower molecules [1]; attractions significant [1] (b) molecular volume significant [1]; intermolecular forces significant [1]

items.stem: Under which conditions would a sample of carbon dioxide behave most like an ideal gas?
items.answer: 100 kPa and 300 K
items.markingKey: Lowest pressure and highest temperature: molecules far apart and fast moving.

items.stem: Under which conditions would a sample of carbon dioxide behave most like an ideal gas?
items.answer: 2000 kPa and 800 K
items.markingKey: Lowest pressure and highest temperature: molecules far apart and fast moving.

items.stem: A gas-supply company in Colombo stores methane at high pressure in steel cylinders. State the conditions under which a real gas behaves most ideally.
items.answer: High temperature and low pressure.
items.markingKey: High temperature and low pressure. [1]

items.stem: Tomás compares the behaviour of helium and ammonia stored in cylinders in a university teaching laboratory. (a) State three assumptions of the kinetic theory for an ideal gas. (b) Explain why the pressure in a cylinder increases if it is left in the sun.
items.answer: (a) Negligible molecular volume; no intermolecular forces; elastic collisions; random motion. (b) Molecules gain kinetic energy, collide with walls more often and harder.
items.markingKey: (a) Negligible molecular volume; no intermolecular forces; elastic collisions; random motion. [3] (b) Molecules gain kinetic energy, collide with walls more often and harder. [2]

items.stem: Which expression gives the relative molecular mass of a gas from the ideal gas equation?
items.answer: M = mRT/pV
items.markingKey: n = m/M = pV/RT, so M = mRT/pV.

items.stem: A student in Cairo uses the ideal gas equation in a set of calculations. Explain why the volatile-liquid (gas syringe) method gives a value of Mr that may be inaccurate for a liquid like ethanol near its boiling point.
items.answer: Near its boiling point the vapour does not behave ideally (strong intermolecular forces/hydrogen bonding), so pV = nRT does not apply exactly.
items.markingKey: non-ideal near boiling point; intermolecular forces significant [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Suggest one source of error when measuring the Mr of a volatile liquid by injecting it into a heated gas syringe. (b) Explain why the volatile-liquid (gas syringe) method gives a value of Mr that may be inaccurate for a liquid like ethanol near its boiling point.
items.answer: (a) Some liquid may not vaporise or may evaporate from the needle before weighing; temperature of the syringe may not be uniform. (b) Near its boiling point the vapour does not behave ideally (strong intermolecular forces/hydrogen bonding), so pV = nRT does not apply exactly.
items.markingKey: (a) identifies error [1]; effect on Mr [1] (b) non-ideal near boiling point [1]; intermolecular forces significant [1]

items.stem: A sample of gas G of mass 0.101 g occupies 150 cm³ at 98.5 kPa and 27 °C. Calculate the relative molecular mass of G. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
Calculate the volume, in cm³, occupied by 0.00802 mol of nitrogen at 100 kPa and 27 °C. (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
items.answer: 200 cm³

items.stem: In a university teaching laboratory in Auckland, 0.160 g of an unknown liquid evaporates completely in a heated syringe, giving 70.0 cm³ of vapour at 383 K and 101 kPa. (a) State the ideal gas equation and the units of each quantity. (b) Calculate the relative molecular mass of the liquid. (c) State one assumption of the ideal gas model that is least valid at high pressure.
items.answer: (a) pV = nRT: p in Pa, V in m³, n in mol, R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T in K. (b) 72.0 (c) Volume of molecules negligible / no intermolecular forces.
items.markingKey: (a) pV = nRT: p in Pa, V in m³, n in mol, R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T in K. [2] (b) 72.0 [1] (c) Volume of molecules negligible / no intermolecular forces. [1]

items.stem: Arjun vaporises 0.160 g of a volatile liquid in a gas syringe at 383 K and 101 kPa. The vapour occupies 70.0 cm³. (a) State the ideal gas equation and the units of each quantity. (b) Calculate the relative molecular mass of the liquid. (c) The liquid is pentane. Suggest why the experimental Mr may differ from the true value. (d) State one assumption of the ideal gas model that is least valid at high pressure.
items.answer: (a) pV = nRT: p in Pa, V in m³, n in mol, R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T in K. (b) 72.0 (c) Vapour non-ideal near boiling point (intermolecular forces); loss of liquid by evaporation; temperature not uniform. (d) Volume of molecules negligible / no intermolecular forces.
items.markingKey: (a) pV = nRT: p in Pa, V in m³, n in mol, R in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T in K. [2] (b) 72.0 [1] (c) Vapour non-ideal near boiling point (intermolecular forces); loss of liquid by evaporation; temperature not uniform. [2] (d) Volume of molecules negligible / no intermolecular forces. [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which substance has a giant covalent structure? (b) What type of lattice does iodine form in the solid state?
items.answer: (a) silicon(IV) oxide (b) simple molecular lattice
items.markingKey: (a) SiO₂: each Si bonded to four O in a 3D network. (b) I₂ molecules held by weak London forces in a regular lattice.

items.stem: A materials scientist in Bogotá is choosing a solid for a high-temperature application. Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.
items.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have higher charges (and are smaller) than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the electrostatic attraction between ions is stronger.
items.markingKey: higher charges/smaller ions; stronger electrostatic attraction [2]

items.stem: A materials scientist in Karachi is choosing a solid for a high-temperature application. (a) Explain why iodine has a low melting point even though the I–I bond is covalent. (b) Explain why magnesium oxide has a much higher melting point than sodium chloride.
items.answer: (a) Melting only overcomes the weak London forces between I₂ molecules; the covalent bonds are not broken. (b) Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have higher charges (and are smaller) than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the electrostatic attraction between ions is stronger.
items.markingKey: (a) weak intermolecular forces; covalent bonds not broken [2] (b) higher charges/smaller ions; stronger electrostatic attraction [2]

items.stem: Solid S has a melting point that is low. It does not conduct electricity when solid and does not conduct when molten or dissolved. It is insoluble in water. Deduce the type of structure in S and explain each property.
items.answer: simple molecular (e.g. sulfur (S₈)): only weak intermolecular forces between molecules need to be overcome; no ions or delocalised electrons.
items.markingKey: structure simple molecular [1]; melting point explained [1]; conductivity explained [1]

items.stem: Jonas is given samples of sodium chloride, magnesium oxide and diamond to classify in a school laboratory. Describe the structure of graphite and explain why it is used in electrodes and as a lubricant.
items.answer: Layers of hexagonal C rings, each C bonded to three others; delocalised electrons conduct; weak forces between layers allow sliding.
items.markingKey: Layers of hexagonal C rings, each C bonded to three others; delocalised electrons conduct; weak forces between layers allow sliding. [3]

items.stem: Sipho is given samples of potassium bromide, sulfur (S₈) and silicon(IV) oxide to classify in a quality-control laboratory. (a) Explain the melting point of potassium bromide. (b) Explain whether sulfur (S₈) conducts electricity as a solid.
items.answer: (a) high (734 °C): strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice; ions are fixed in the solid but mobile when molten or dissolved. (b) No: only weak intermolecular forces between molecules need to be overcome; no ions or delocalised electrons.
items.markingKey: (a) high (734 °C): strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions throughout the lattice; ions are fixed in the solid but mobile when molten or dissolved.
